label: Consumerism and Stuff
framing: The ad does not sell you a thing. It sells you a self you do not yet have, and tells you the gap can be closed with a purchase. Scripture answers not with a tighter budget but with a deeper word, that a life does not consist in the abundance of possessions.
cultural: We have built an economy that runs on a permanent sense of lack, that needs us to want what we do not have in order to keep moving. The deal is never named out loud. We feel it in the small dissatisfaction that arrives the week after the package does, and we reach for the next one.
historical: The early church in Acts startled Rome by holding goods loosely and sharing them, in a world that measured a person by what he owned. Basil of Caesarea in the fourth century told the rich that the coat hanging unused in their closet belonged to the naked, and John Wesley in the eighteenth century, growing wealthy from his books, kept his own spending fixed and gave the rest away.
application: Before the next purchase, wait a week and see whether the want survives the silence. Practice giving a fixed portion first, so generosity sets the shape of your money rather than what is left over. And take a slow inventory of what you already own, since gratitude for what is here is the only real cure for the hunger that is never fed.

verses.text: When the woman saw that the tree was good for food and pleasing to the eyes, and that it was desirable for obtaining wisdom, she took the fruit and ate it. She also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate it.
verses.where: The woman sees that the tree is good for food, pleasing to the eyes and desirable for wisdom, and she takes and eats, and gives to her husband, who eats. The site's note says sin works through goods rightly made, food, beauty and wisdom all being God's gifts, and the wrong lies in seizing them against his word. The plain note says temptation begins with a question about God's goodness: is he holding out on you?

verses.text: Do not love the world or anything in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. For all that is in the world—the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes, and the pride of life—is not from the Father but from the world. The world is passing away, along with its desires; but whoever does the will of God remains forever.
verses.where: John warns against loving the world, which he describes as the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes and the pride of life, all passing away. The site's plain note says the world here means a way of life set against God, not God's good creation or the people in it, and that John's point is not letting appetite, envy or pride take God's place. It asks what you are building your life on that is passing away.

verses.text: Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied; so the eyes of man are never satisfied.
verses.where: As the grave is never satisfied, so the eyes of man are never satisfied. The site's note on the chapter says it gathers sayings on the restless human appetite. The proverb sets the eye's hunger beside the grave's, one more thing that always has room for more.

verses.text: All a man’s labor is for his mouth, yet his appetite is never satisfied. What advantage, then, has the wise man over the fool? What gain comes to the poor man who knows how to conduct himself before others? Better what the eye can see than the wandering of desire. This too is futile and a pursuit of the wind.
verses.where: The Teacher says all a person's labour is for the mouth, yet the appetite is never satisfied, and better what the eye can see than the wandering of desire. The site's note on the chapter says it describes a man who has riches, wealth and honor and cannot enjoy them, and that appetite is never satisfied. Having and enjoying are not the same thing.

verses.text: Do not be amazed when a man grows rich, when the splendor of his house increases. For when he dies, he will carry nothing away; his abundance will not follow him down.
verses.where: Do not be amazed when someone grows rich and the splendour of his house increases, the psalm says, for he will carry nothing away. The site's plain note says the difference in this psalm is not between rich and poor, and asks whether you have understanding about what you own. Hold it, the note says, the way someone holds a thing they will have to leave.

verses.text: You lie on beds inlaid with ivory, and lounge upon your couches. You dine on lambs from the flock and calves from the stall. You improvise songs on the harp like David and invent your own musical instruments. You drink wine by the bowlful and anoint yourselves with the finest oils, but you fail to grieve over the ruin of Joseph.
verses.where: Amos pictures the comfortable elite on ivory beds, eating the best lambs, drinking wine by the bowlful, and failing to grieve over the ruin of Joseph. The site's note says Amos is not condemning feasting, music or wine as such, which Scripture celebrates as God's gifts, but luxury gained through injustice and enjoyed in complacency. The chapter asks whether enjoyment has made a person unable to see or feel what is happening to others.

verses.text: Your riches have rotted and moths have eaten your clothes. Your gold and silver are corroded. Their corrosion will testify against you and consume your flesh like fire. You have hoarded treasure in the last days.
verses.where: James tells rich landowners that their riches have rotted, their clothes are moth-eaten and their gold corroded, because they hoarded treasure. The site's note on the chapter says they hoarded wealth, withheld wages and condemned the innocent. The plain note asks how the people who make what you buy are paid.

verses.text: Then Jesus looked around and said to His disciples, “How hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of God!” And the disciples were amazed at His words. But Jesus said to them again, “Children, how hard it is to enter the kingdom of God! It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.”
verses.where: Jesus says how hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of God, easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle. The site's note says he does not call riches sinful but says they supply the security the kingdom asks a person to give up, and that the camel was a recognized way of speaking of the impossible, not a gate or a rope. The plain note asks what you trust to make you safe, and says the answer of verse 27 is for everyone: all things are possible with God.

verses.text: You have planted much but harvested little. You eat but never have enough. You drink but never have your fill. You put on clothes but never get warm. You earn wages to put into a bag pierced through.”
verses.where: Haggai tells the people that they eat but never have enough, put on clothes but never get warm, and earn wages to put into a bag with holes. The site's note on the chapter says they were living in panelled houses while the temple lay in ruins, and its hard note warns against turning this into a rule that every hardship has a simple spiritual cause. What carries over is the call to consider your ways.

verses.text: Then Jesus said to His disciples, “Therefore I tell you, do not worry about your life, what you will eat, or about your body, what you will wear. For life is more than food, and the body more than clothes.
verses.where: Jesus tells his disciples not to worry about what they will eat or wear, for life is more than food and the body more than clothes. The site's note says the rich fool was anxious to secure too much and disciples may be anxious about securing enough, and both are answered by trust in the Father. The plain note says your heart follows your treasure: look where your money and time go, and you will see where your heart is.

links.label: Practical guides for life in the world

misread.taken: I have come that they may have life in all its fullness is quoted as if Jesus promised a full life in the sense the advertisements mean: more comfort, more possessions, a better house and a better car.
misread.says: The site's note says the life Jesus gives is the eternal life of the whole Gospel, and its abundance is not wealth or comfort but fullness of relationship with God, given at the cost of the shepherd's own life. The plain note sets the verse against voices that come to take, your money, your loyalty, your time, and leave you emptier than they found you; Jesus says he came to give.
misread.text: The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I have come that they may have life, and have it in all its fullness.

whole: Most people in rich countries do not feel rich. They feel behind. The phone is two years old, the kitchen looks tired next to a friend's, the children want what their classmates have, and every screen offers something that will make life easier, more beautiful or more like someone else's. Shopping can become a way to cope with a bad day, a reward for a hard week, or a way to feel in control. The cupboards fill, the storage units fill, the debt grows, and the satisfaction lasts about as long as the packaging. Many people know this and still cannot stop.

Scripture saw this long before advertising. Eve saw that the fruit was good for food, pleasing to the eye and desirable, and the site's note says sin works through goods rightly made by seizing them against God's word. Proverbs says the eyes of man are never satisfied, and the Teacher describes a man with riches and honor who cannot enjoy them, because appetite is never full. John names the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes and the pride of life, and says they are passing away. Underneath is the same question the serpent asked, whether God is holding out on us, and the same promise that the next thing will finally fill the gap. It never does. The site's note on Ecclesiastes 3 says God has set eternity in human hearts, and a heart with eternity in it is not filled by the next purchase.

So the Bible's wisdom does not despise good things. Amos condemned not feasting and music but luxury bought by injustice and enjoyed while others fell apart, and Jesus told his followers that life is more than food and the body more than clothes. In practice that means looking honestly at where the money and time go, since the heart follows them. It means asking, as James does, how the people who made what we buy are paid. It means enjoying what we have without needing the next thing, giving some of it away, and holding the rest the way the psalm says, like something we will have to leave. And it means noticing the bag with holes in it, the wages that never seem to stay, and considering our ways.

The hope Scripture gives is a fullness no shop can sell. Jesus came that his sheep might have life in all its fullness, and the note says that fullness is relationship with God, given at the cost of the shepherd's own life. Taste and see that the LORD is good, the psalm says; those who seek him lack no good thing. A person who has tasted that can walk past the window without needing what is in it.
deep.sit: What did you last buy hoping it would make you feel better, and what were you really hoping for?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note says taste and see is an invitation, not an argument: you cannot know a food by reading about it, and the psalm asks you to try trusting God and find out.
prayer.text: Taste and see that the LORD is good; blessed is the man who takes refuge in Him! Fear the LORD, you His saints, for those who fear Him lack nothing. Young lions go lacking and hungry, but those who seek the LORD lack no good thing.
